desc:
A positive integer is a factorion when it equals the sum of the factorials of its own decimal digits. For example 145 is a factorion, because 1! + 4! + 5! = 1 + 24 + 120 = 145.

Given n, return every factorion from 1 to n inclusive, in increasing order. Remember that 0! = 1.

n = 100    -> [1, 2]
n = 145    -> [1, 2, 145]
n = 50000  -> [1, 2, 145, 40585]
hints: Testing every number up to n is too slow near two billion. Ask how large a factorion can be compared with its number of digits.
The largest digit factorial is 9! = 362,880, so a number with d digits can equal a sum of digit factorials only if it is at most d * 362,880.
Since 10<sup>d-1</sup> must not exceed d * 362,880, factorions have at most 7 digits. Enumerate the digit multisets of those sizes and keep the sums whose own digits are exactly that multiset.
editorial: If x has d digits, then x is at least 10<sup>d-1</sup>, while the sum of the factorials of its digits is at most d * 9! = d * 362,880. For d = 8 the first quantity is 10,000,000 and the second is 2,903,040, so no factorion has 8 or more digits.

So instead of scanning the numbers, scan the multisets of digits of size 1 to 8. For each multiset, compute s as the sum of the factorials of its digits. The multiset is the digit multiset of a factorion exactly when s has the same digits as the multiset. Each factorion comes from exactly one multiset, and a set removes any repeats.
There are only about 48,000 such multisets, so the work does not depend on n. The result for any n up to 2<sup>31</sup> - 1 is simply the filtered list 1, 2, 145, 40585.
time: O(M * d), M about 48,000 digit multisets
